statement: When building a distributed key-value store, start with a single MySQL node and do not think about distribution on day zero: first cover all the implementation details ('devils') on one node, sort them out, then scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: no, don't think about distributed on day zero, it's that simple

statement: The single-node schema is a table called store with columns key, value, TTL (the absolute expiration time) and is_deleted (for soft delete).
detail: The teacher notes these columns come 'so naturally' and then questions whether every column is really needed for storage.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So we add a simple schema called store: we have key, we have value, we store the TTL, we store is deleted.

statement: Engineers are habituated to adding an auto-increment ID column to every table, but you do not always need one; add it only in case you need it.
detail: The teacher attributes the habit to ORMs: an ID column makes the ORM's life simple.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we are habituated into having an ID column, auto increment, for some reason

statement: The teacher's opinion: ORMs suck and he hates them; people keep an ID column because it makes the ORM's life simple.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ORM sucks, I hate them.

statement: Instead of a separate soft-delete column, use the special value -1 in the absolute expiration time (TTL) column to mark a key as deleted; this saves the space of the extra column.
detail: Final schema: key, value, TTL (absolute expiration time). The -1 also makes the hard delete simpler.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you use a special value minus one in expiration, in TTL, in the absolute expiration time

statement: A user delete is actually an update (setting expiration to -1); a periodic job later batches the hard deletes, so the database has to do minimal B+ tree rebalancing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is where your database has to do minimal B+ tree rebalancing.

statement: A put must be an upsert, not an insert: when the same key is put twice, the second value is expected to replace the first.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: cannot be an insert, it has to be an upsert

statement: Implementing put by first getting the value and then inserting or updating is 'pathetic' and slows the system down by a massive margin.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It would slow down your system by a massive [?margin | asr: "barge"].

statement: Upsert syntax depends on the database: in MySQL replace INSERT with REPLACE (INSERT INTO store VALUES ... becomes REPLACE INTO); in Postgres replace INSERT with UPSERT.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: replace insert with replace, that is upsert in MySQL, and replace insert with upsert, that is upsert in Postgres

statement: To handle multiple concurrent put requests on the same key, leverage the locks just studied or play with isolation levels: the SQL database already gives these guarantees, so you do not have to reimplement them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because SQL database already gives you these guarantees, you can just leverage them

statement: One option for concurrent puts is to take an exclusive lock with FOR UPDATE NOWAIT, so a put fails immediately ('kill myself') if someone else is updating the key, and then do the update.
detail: The teacher says he picked NOWAIT 'just for fancy', hypothetically, with no specific reason.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: just take exclusive lock for update no wait

statement: There is no right way to choose between SKIP LOCKED, NOWAIT or plain waiting for concurrent puts: it depends on the guarantees you want your database to provide.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is no right way to do it, it depends on the guarantees that you want your database to provide.

statement: TTL approach 1 (batch deletion with a cron job): every 10 minutes trigger a hard deletion that fires DELETE FROM store WHERE expired_at < now.
detail: The teacher announces multiple TTL approaches: first batch/cron, then how Redis does it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So approach one, we do batch deletion with cron job. So every 10 minutes we trigger a hard deletion

statement: Because an expired key still exists until the next hard-deletion job runs, get must filter it in SQL: SELECT * FROM store WHERE key = k AND expired_at > now.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It should be select star from store where key equal to k and expired at

statement: Filtering expired keys in the get query avoids moving the value to the user and filtering it there: it saves the network bandwidth of the server and of the database, and the disk IO time the database spends reading a humongous value.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It saves the network bandwidth of the server. It saves the network bandwidth of the database.

statement: Such micro-optimizations make a database far more performant.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And this micro-optimizations make your database far more [?performant | asr: "proper"].

statement: Lazy deletion: in an in-memory database such as Redis, when a key that is accessed (get) is found to be expired, it is deleted immediately, without proactively going to delete it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is called lazy deletion.

statement: Almost all in-memory databases do lazy deletion; it applies to in-memory databases, not the disk-based one built so far.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And almost all in-memory databases do that.

statement: In memory, deleting a key is cheap: there is no tree to rebalance and no network IO penalty; it is just freeing memory (malloc/free, new/delete in C/C++) and removing the key from the hash table.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You malloc, you free [?stuff | asr: "stop"], right?

statement: Do not do lazy (per-key) deletion on an on-disk database: every micro delete requires rebalancing the B+ tree, which is pathetically slow.
detail: The teacher stresses he is 'iterating it 100 times'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every micro delete operations requires rebalancing of B+ tree, pathetically slow

statement: On disk you do batch deletion; in memory you can do pointed (or staggered) deletions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So that's why you do batch deletion when you are on disk. When you are in memory, you can do pointed deletions or staggered deletions

statement: Redis does lazy deletion: if a key with a TTL is read before Redis's periodic cleanup has removed it, Redis does not return it, tells the user the key does not exist, and deletes it right there because that is not an expensive operation for it.
detail: Redis runs the cleanup not as a thread but 'kind of' asynchronously; the teacher says he cannot reveal details because he covers them in his course and they are out of scope.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it tells to the user that key does not exist

statement: Redis hard-deletes a key in two cases: when the user tells it to delete the key, and when it accesses a key that is expired but not yet deleted (lazy deletion).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I would delete a key, hard delete a key, either when user tells me to hard delete a key

statement: Lazy deletion alone leaves keys that expire but are never accessed, so a periodic job is still needed; Redis's regular job does not hard-delete all the expired keys.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now what Redis does as part of this regular job is that it does not do hard deletes of all the keys.

statement: Redis's expiry merges two approaches: lazy deletion on access plus a periodic job.
detail: The teacher calls it a very beautiful, simple algorithm that uses a bit of math.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it takes up two approaches and merges it

statement: The natural periodic job deletes all expired-but-not-deleted keys each run, but with millions of such keys this takes a lot of time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's say there are millions of keys like that, it takes up a lot of time to delete those large number of keys

statement: Lazy deletion solves about 90% of the expiry problem, because there is a very high chance an expired key gets accessed, is hard-deleted and frees memory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So that solves 90% of the problem.

statement: Redis's periodic expiry job samples exactly 20 random keys among those with an expiration set and deletes the ones in the sample that are expired, instead of deleting all expired keys.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis samples exactly 20 keys that has some expiration set

statement: Sampling-based expiry is not suitable for a disk-based database; it works only for an in-memory database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: again, not suitable for disk-based database, only for in-memory database you can do this

statement: If more than 25% of the 20 sampled keys were expired and deleted, Redis repeats the sampling; it stops when fewer than 25% of the sample were deleted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if the number of deleted keys from the sample are more than 25%, then you repeat the process

statement: Statistics behind the sampling: the population is the whole Redis key set with expiration; a random sample of 20 should be representative of it, so if 50% of the sample is expired, roughly 50% of the population is expired.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: sample should be representative of population

statement: Example: if in one iteration only 3 of the 20 sampled keys are expired (15%), Redis deletes those 3 and stops; about 15% of the population is then expired but not deleted, and that is okay.
detail: The remaining ~10% not covered by lazy deletion is handled 'eventually' by this sampling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: out of this 20 only three keys are expired

statement: Redis optimizes for speed, not completeness: spending a lot of time on cleanup would leave less time for reads and writes, because Redis is single threaded.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis optimizes for speed and not completeness of the system

statement: Redis is single threaded: there are no multiple threads running anywhere in Redis, so it cannot hand cleanup to another thread and must keep cleanup time minimal to handle actual commands (get, put, delete).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because Redis is single threaded. There is no multiple threads in Redis running anywhere.

statement: Expired-but-not-deleted keys statistically consume only 20-25% of Redis's total memory, and that is the worst case, since lazy deletion does the bulk of the deletion.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Statistically speaking, it would consume only 20-25% of the total consumption of the memory.

statement: Redis samples exactly 20 keys (not 15, 21 or 30) because of the central limit theorem; the proof is in a paper that is also tagged on Redis's website.
detail: Teacher: if you like math go explore it; otherwise just remember it is exactly 20 keys.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because of central limit theorem.

statement: The 20-key sampling works up until 5 million keys.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It works for up until 5 million keys

statement: There is no one way to build a system: whatever works for you, works for you.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is no one way to build a system

statement: Redis trades a bit of memory leak for speed, assuming the leftover expired keys are eventually cleaned up through lazy deletion and random sampling, so it spends bare minimum time in its periodic job.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis is optimizing for speed by trading off a bit of memory leak

statement: Delete micro-optimization: the delete query UPDATE store SET TTL = -1 WHERE key = K1 should also include AND TTL > now, so a key is soft-deleted only when it is not already expired.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So set, or delete a key, only when it is not expired.

statement: The 'TTL > now' clause saves disk IO: an already-expired key does not need its row updated, so the update does no disk IO for it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this update would not do a disk IO if the key is already expired, because of this clause

statement: The clause saves two disk IOs per such delete, because there is also an index on TTL that would otherwise be updated.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you are saving two disk IOs by adding this one clause.

statement: The teacher found this delete clause in Apache Ignite, wondered why it was there, mimicked the load, and then realized it was a nice optimization.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is what I found in Apache Ignite.

statement: Do disk IO only when it is needed; otherwise do not do it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you do the disk IO only when it is needed

statement: Final queries: batch cleanup is DELETE FROM store WHERE TTL <= now; get is SELECT * FROM store WHERE key = K1 AND TTL > now, so you never make a network IO for something already expired.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: delete from store where TTL is less than equal to now

statement: Why set TTL to -1 on delete instead of just relying on the batch job: if a key has no TTL it never expires, so when a user explicitly deletes it you have to do something in the database; the -1 marks it.
detail: A student argued that expired_at already holds date and time, so the batch job compares with now and no update is needed; the teacher's answer covers keys without TTL that are explicitly deleted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if TTL is not set for a key, then key was never expired.
flags: check: speaker boundary - "deleting it how would you do it" may be the Teacher
check: speaker boundary - "okay so that can cause issues ... even if you're doing" may be the Teacher
check: speaker boundary - "I'm writing it now. Should I write the actual time there?" may be the student

statement: Instead of -1, the deleted marker can be any magic value, e.g. a date earlier than 1 January 1970 (if expired_at is a date-time or epoch timestamp).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: change this minus one to some magic value,
flags: check: speaker boundary - "let's say first January 1970. That works." may be the Teacher

statement: The disk IO savings of these queries rely on having an index on the TTL (expired_at) column; without it the database would read the rows anyway.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: You'd have that index.
flags: check: Teacher called "Pankaj" just before; name spelling

statement: A student proposed an in-memory append-only layer in front of the database to reduce insert IO; the teacher said this is just adding a cache in front, which you can do, but it is not the core transactional database itself.
detail: The student also mentioned a Bloom filter and flushing to disk from time to time.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: You are just adding a cache in front of it.

statement: An in-memory layer in front of the store is limited by memory: all the keys need to fit in memory (and must be flushed from time to time).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But then you are limited by memory where all the keys needs to fit in memory.

statement: Two of such performance optimizations will be covered in the fifth and sixth week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll be touching upon two of those in fifth and sixth week.

statement: The store is made distributed when one node cannot handle the load: high network IO, disk, a large amount of data stored, or a large number of queries fired.
detail: As discussed last week, 'handle' is not just query or storage.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One node is not able to handle the load of it.

statement: Basic one-node architecture: user -> load balancer -> KV API servers -> MySQL; anyone who wants to talk to the database goes through the API servers, and a separate job continuously fires the batch cleanup queries on MySQL.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: User, load balancer, API servers.

statement: As long as MySQL can sustain the load, handle more requests by adding more API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: all we have to just add more API servers

statement: When MySQL cannot sustain the load, first go through the access pattern: use metrics on which queries are fired more (select, update, upsert or delete).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you first go through the access pattern

statement: If reads dominate, spin up replicas of the database; replicas mean allowing some staleness, which is okay for some use cases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you spin up replicas of this DB. And when you do replicas, you are allowing some staleness in the data

statement: Consistent reads, updates and deletes go to the master; data replicates asynchronously to replicas; reads that tolerate a little staleness can go directly to a replica.
detail: Exactly what was discussed last week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if consistent reads go to master, updates go to master, delete go to master, data asynchronously replicates on the replica

statement: Simplest implementation: the KV API servers create connections to both master and replicas and pick one per request depending on the kind of read the client asks for; no central proxy, complications added later.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: not adding central proxy, nothing complication, we will add a complication later

statement: When one master can no longer handle the write load, first try to scale vertically; when that is not possible, shard the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you first try to vertically scale up. When you cannot do that, then you shard your database.

statement: Sharding means having exclusive copies (disjoint portions) of the data across databases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's literally having exclusive copy of data across databases

statement: Range sharding example: if keys are strings A to Z, one master handles A to M and another handles N to Z; each master may have its own set of replicas.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have one master that handles A to M and another master that handles N to Z

statement: Each shard master has its own batch cleanup job running independently.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Each master will have its own batch cleanup job independently running.

statement: KV API servers hold connections to all masters and replicas; minimizing the number of connections through intelligent balancing is a different problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: that's intelligent balancing that you may want to do

statement: Routing example: a request for Google's stock price goes to master one because Google starts with G; a request for Zomato's goes to the other master.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Google starts with a G, I would have to fire a query on master one to get it.

statement: The routing information (which database holds which key range) is kept at the KV API server side, which picks the database connection for each request.
detail: Called a simplistic implementation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we are keeping this information, the routing information at the API server side itself

statement: Hot partitions, adding replicas on the fly and scaling dynamically will be discussed in depth in the fifth, sixth and seventh weeks.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we would discuss fifth week, sixth week and seventh week a lot in depth

statement: Request flow: each database is a master with replicas; the KV API holds connections to all of them; for a key it looks up which range holds it, sends the query through that connection, gets the response and returns it to the user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: KV API knows where to forward it to because it's just a range that it stores

statement: About 90% of sharded databases work like this (fixed ranges with routing), because very few real-world use cases need to dynamically add or remove shards.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in most cases, like 90% of sharded databases work like this

statement: Changing the number of shards is typically a one-time activity happening about once every quarter, so it can be done explicitly without over-complicating the system.
detail: Dynamic resharding, consistent hashing and hot partitions come in week five.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's typically in one-time activity, happening once every quarter

statement: If two shards can no longer handle the load, add one more node and split the key range into three parts.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We add one more and we split this range into three parts

statement: Resulting distributed setup: several masters each with replicas handling read load, writes and critical reads to the master, a batch cleanup job per master, and all routing information in the KV API.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: all the routing information is with KV API

statement: Do not over-complicate the problem at first; keep it really simple.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So not over complicating the problem at first.

statement: Recommended exercise: implement this locally (no cloud needed) with two MySQL servers on your machine, one API server connected to both, routing logic, and an HTTP endpoint that routes requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Just spin up a MySQL server, two MySQL servers, local machine, right?

statement: Stretch goal of the exercise (last step): create a replica locally using MySQL binlog (or Postgres's commit log), connect the KV API to it, and route critical reads to the master.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: MySQL binlog if you're using MySQL

statement: Implementing it yourself is how you understand it much better; it is not difficult - implement the replica and the routing layer once and things become clear.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you implement it, with understand it much better, right?

statement: Week five will cover hot partitions, dynamic scaling and partitioning, consistent hashing (where it sucks and where it is good) and three ways to handle the hot partition problem; it needs prerequisites first.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: hot partition problem, three ways to handle it

statement: The 'TTL > now' condition in the delete query is not the batch delete; it is the delete operation triggered by a user, which only soft-deletes keys that are not yet expired.
detail: A student confused it with the batch cleanup condition (TTL < now).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, this is not batch delete, this is delete operation by a user.

statement: The TTL column here is expired_at: the absolute time at which the key expires (e.g. 12 o'clock on a particular day), not a duration.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: TTL is expired at, the absolute time of expiration

statement: User delete sets TTL to a magic number only where the key is not yet expired; batch delete is a separate cleanup that hard-deletes keys whose TTL is less than now.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Updating, setting TTL to a magical value, to a magic number, where it is not yet expired.

statement: A user delete does not hard-delete the key every time, because that would require rebalancing the B+ tree; the hard delete happens later in batch.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are not going ahead and deleting the key, hard deleting every time, otherwise it would require rebalancing of binary trees

statement: Even though the update is fired for every user delete, it leads to no disk IO for already-expired keys because the clause does not match them; those are handled by the batch cleanup ('heads you win, tails you win').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it would not lead to any disk IO for expired keys

statement: If the underlying MySQL provides ACID and the KV store is not partitioned, the KV store gives the same ACID guarantees.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: Yes, we do. Sure.
flags: check: "Sidesh?" may be the Teacher calling on a student; name spelling

statement: Key-value databases give key-based operations; once partitioned you cannot have ACID guarantees across partitions (e.g. a transaction over four keys where three are on one shard and one on another).
detail: The student raised the airline example of a multi-key transaction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You cannot have ACID guarantees across partitions.

statement: Distributed transactions reduce performance by a huge margin, so you typically do not use them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: distributed transactions, they reduce your performance by a huge margin

statement: ACID can still be guaranteed within a shard, as long as all the keys an operation touches lie on the same node.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: so long as all the keys that I'm performing operations on lie on the same node

statement: Asked how an IIT Delhi student's app achieved faster bookings some years back, the teacher said he has no idea.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: No idea about it.

statement: To mock the distributed system locally, focus on what matters: one database and one replica running locally with your app; do not go into autoscaling or the same CRUD work again and again.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Just your local machine, one database running locally, one replica running locally, that's it.

statement: In Redis's sampling, the 25% threshold is on the keys deleted from the sample (the expired ones in the 20-key sample), not on an expired-keys count over the whole database, which would itself be a slow operation.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: Delete all the keys that are expired from the sample, and you deleted keys are more than 25%, you repeat the process.
flags: unclear: "It is finding good folks. Not listen."

statement: Sampling operates only on the small sample, not on the database, because at any time there may be millions of expired-but-not-deleted keys; the trade-off is that some expired keys remain, but not more than 25% since the sample represents the population.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there would not be more than 25 percent of that, because sample represents the population

statement: A student suggested sampling fails on a disk-backed DB because you would fetch all records and then filter the top N (and deletion needs rebalancing).
detail: Teacher's correction of the first point: you need not fetch all rows and then sample; you can pick 20 random rows, but picking those 20 at random is the expensive part.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we will be getting all the records and then filtering out top N number of records

statement: On disk, picking 20 random keys requires 20 random disk IOs reading disk pages from anywhere on disk, which is very slow; in memory random picks are very easy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it would require you to do 20 random disk IOs, very slow

statement: On a disk-based database it is much better to just skim through the rows and delete what is expired than to do random sampling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It would be much better if you just skim through the rows and delete what you, at this point, delete what is expired

statement: Autocommit = true means a standalone SQL statement is committed on its own; inside an explicit BEGIN ... COMMIT transaction the commit happens at the end, so FOR UPDATE locks work as shown regardless of autocommit.
detail: The teacher first says autocommit is true for the shell.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: But if you just fire one standalone SQL statement, that would be committed. That's what auto commit true means.

statement: In the FOR UPDATE booking approach, the N(N+1)/2 figure counts evaluations of queries done internally by the database (each waiting thread re-evaluates after the locked seat is taken), not queries fired by the application.
detail: Student recap: with 120 threads, all wait on seat 1, then 119 wait on seat 2, and so on.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Not queries, evaluation of queries.
flags: unclear: "from RN would still fire inquiries"
check: possibly the Teacher interjecting ("One would move forward")

statement: With SKIP LOCKED the database does not re-evaluate the query: it reads a whole disk page (one B+ tree node, possibly hundreds of rows), and if the first row is locked it immediately moves to the next one.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It reads one disk page, that one disk page, one B+ tree node may contain hundreds of rows.

statement: A student concluded that with SKIP LOCKED only about 120 evaluations (one per thread) are triggered.

speaker: student (proposal)

statement: LIMIT (and OFFSET) is applied at the last step, when results are being accumulated and filtered, not before the disk read.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It happens at the last step when you are filtering it out.

statement: ORMs do not always generate optimal queries and are bad at advanced SQL queries.
detail: For why ORMs suck, Google it; there are tons of articles (Hacker News).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ORM does not generate optimal queries.
flags: check: words may be lost before "hard you try"

statement: ORMs make life simple and give speed but take away control; for example they lack good support for invoking an optimized query placed in a stored procedure.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ORMs do not have a great support for that.

statement: ORMs are good for mid-scale; at high scale, when you want micro-optimizations and control over SQL query creation, ORMs are the worst.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ORMs are good for mid-scale.

statement: A startup should use an ORM: the teacher uses ORMs day in and day out, they increase shipping velocity at an early stage, and over-optimizing would slow you down; but at scale he would not use one.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you're a startup, you should use ORM

statement: An ORM deprives you of raw performance: for example it selects all columns by default, and the explicit projections needed to get performance make the code unreadable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it always has to select all the columns by default

statement: A SQL query is more readable than the equivalent ORM code; Django's prefetch_related and similar features, and Hibernate, are an 'utter mess'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You would feel like SQL query is more readable than your ORM junk.

statement: ORMs are built for general use cases across databases (MySQL, Postgres, ...), so a query construct only one database offers may not be supported; then you write a raw query / prepared statement.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if I want to leverage a particular query construct that only MySQL offers, ORM might not have support for that

statement: ORMs also suck at connection pooling; the teacher has had his fair share of problems with ORMs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: connection pooling, or plus basically connection to use ORM. Suck at that also.

statement: Writing native SQL queries inside the ORM for the bigger queries is a good compromise ('100%'), because ORMs do not give raw performance or database-specific operations, and complex ORM queries hurt readability.
speaker: student (proposal)

statement: Checking existence with SELECT TOP 1 1 ... WHERE condition and then doing an insert or update still costs an extra round trip: request/response for the select plus request/response for the write, i.e. four network trips versus two with upsert.
detail: The student had seen this pattern in production systems.

statement: 'Lock wait timeout exceeded' means a transaction waited too long for another transaction holding the lock to commit or abort, and that did not happen within the stipulated time.
detail: A student said it happens only when the first transaction took the lock and did not commit; the teacher said 'not really, it is just about timeout'.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: It just about timeout.

statement: Two causes of lock wait timeouts: the lock holder genuinely does a long processing job (then increase the timeout), or processing finished but the code forgot to commit or abort.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So two reasons: either the processing is happening

statement: Why not hard-delete immediately instead of setting -1: every delete may put the B+ tree out of shape and force an expensive rebalance; pointed deletes on a database are very expensive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every time you delete, your B+ tree may go out of shape, it needs to rebalance.

statement: Because pointed deletions are expensive for almost all databases, almost all databases do soft deletes followed by batch cleanups.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So almost all databases do soft deletes and then do batch cleanups.

statement: Read about B+ tree rebalancing (the teacher's video covers it; it was also discussed last week): why it happens and what problems it leads to in databases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So read about B+ tree rebalancing.

statement: Redis does not delegate lazy deletes to a cron job because invoking free on an object is very lightweight (microseconds, no B+ tree rebalancing); delegating might itself be more expensive than deleting right there, especially in in-memory databases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because invoking a free on an object is very lightweight.

statement: Deleting from Redis's array-based hash table just marks that slot as free space.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are just marking that as free space

statement: Deleting immediately frees memory right away; if deletion is delayed to a later cycle and Redis is at full capacity, new inserts that could have succeeded are rejected while expired data still consumes memory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if your Redis is operating at full capacity and you delete bunch of keys and it is waiting for the next cycle to come in

statement: Relational databases do not provide soft deletion out of the box because a database is a fundamental layer: it gives the necessary building blocks (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, SKIP LOCKED, NOWAIT) and does not intervene in the user's space, since otherwise there is no clear line on what to implement.
speaker: student (question)

statement: Built-in soft deletion would need a separate batch cleanup process and would put cognitive load on developers (what if data is not yet deleted, what if I read it, do I use this column?).

statement: DynamoDB always soft-deletes when you delete a key (never a hard delete); for key-value stores soft deletion is foundational, so they provide it, unlike relational databases.
detail: The teacher first named Redis and DynamoDB, then corrected himself to DynamoDB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you delete a key in DynamoDB, it does not hard delete. It always soft deletes.

statement: Around 2011-2012 (the teacher's final year) there was a MySQL forum thread where someone proposed built-in soft deletion; the essence of the reply was that as a database evolves it is more important to know what you do not want to do than what you want to do, since anything is infinitely buildable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it is more important to know what you don't want to do versus what you want to do

statement: When designing a database, always keep in mind what you definitely do not want to do and avoid entering the user's space; give raw constructs to build on.
